Caesar notices: Brutus's angry brow, Calpurnia's pale cheek, Cicero's fiery eyes
'Lean and hungry look': ambitious, discontented, always scheming
Cassius: reads much, great observer, loves no plays, hears no music, seldom smiles
Caesar confides in Antony; deaf ear; Antony was wrong — Cassius led the conspiracy

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

"What a duffer he must think me!" said Hughie, as he was going downstairs. "Not at all," answered Trevor, "I think he is the most charming model I ever had."

(i) Who is 'he'? Describe his appearance when Hughie first saw him in Trevor's studio.
(ii) Why does Hughie feel embarrassed when he says 'What a duffer he must think me!'?
(iii) What is Alan Trevor's profession? Explain the irony in his remark about poverty being picturesque.
(iv) What does the Baron send Hughie later, and why? What is the significance of the word 'model' in the title?
modelAnswer:
(i) 'He' is Baron Hausberg, a fabulously wealthy man who was posing in Trevor's studio disguised as a beggar. When Hughie first saw him, the Baron had the appearance of a wizened old man, with a face like wrinkled parchment, dressed in a tattered brown cloak, with broken and patched boots and a battered hat — the very picture of destitute poverty.
(ii) Hughie feels embarrassed because he had felt so sorry for the supposed beggar that he gave him his last sovereign — only to discover later from Trevor that the 'beggar' was actually the multi-millionaire Baron Hausberg. He is mortified at having given money to one of the richest men in Europe.
(iii) Alan Trevor is a painter. The irony in his remark about poverty being 'picturesque' is that he treats human misery and destitution as aesthetically interesting subject matter — something beautiful to paint — without any real concern for the suffering involved. He exploits poverty for art while ignoring its reality.
(iv) The Baron sends Hughie a cheque for £10,000 as a wedding present for Hughie and Laura, along with a note calling it a 'model' gift from a 'model' millionaire. The word 'model' is significant on two levels: literally, the Baron was Trevor's model (the subject he painted), and figuratively, he is a 'model' — ideal or exemplary — millionaire because he uses his wealth generously and kindly, rewarding Hughie's selfless generosity.
keyPoints: Baron Hausberg — posed as beggar; wizened, wrinkled, tattered cloak, broken boots, battered hat
Hughie gave his last sovereign to a disguised multi-millionaire — mortified
Trevor is a painter; irony: treats poverty as picturesque art, ignoring real suffering
Baron sends £10,000 cheque as wedding gift
'Model': literally a painter's model; figuratively an ideal, exemplary millionaire

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

"For a boy of fourteen Phatik was quite as much trouble as he could be."

(i) Why did Phatik's mother agree to send him to Calcutta with his uncle Bishamber? What does this reveal about her attitude to Phatik?
(ii) How did Phatik fare at school in Calcutta? How did his classmates and his uncle's family treat him?
(iii) Describe Phatik's anguish during his time in Calcutta. What finally happened to him?
(iv) What do Phatik's last words, 'Mother, the holidays have come', suggest about his state of mind?
modelAnswer:
(i) Phatik's mother agreed to send him to Calcutta because his mischief had become unmanageable — he was a constant trouble at home. When Bishamber offered to take him, she readily accepted, almost relieved to be rid of him. This reveals that she found Phatik burdensome and unwanted; she had little affection or patience for her own son.
(ii) At school in Calcutta, Phatik was dull and backward in his lessons and was beaten by his teacher. He could not keep up with his classmates, who mocked him for his ignorance. At home, his uncle's wife treated him with cold indifference, seeing him as an unwanted extra burden — an intrusion on the family.
(iii) Phatik's anguish arose from multiple sources: intense homesickness, his aunt's unkindness, repeated failures and beatings at school, and the humiliation of losing his school books. Eventually, burning with fever and unable to bear his misery, he ran away into the rain, wandered about lost, and was found collapsed. He was brought back seriously ill.
(iv) Phatik's last words — 'Mother, the holidays have come' — suggest that in his delirium he believed he was finally going home to his mother. They reveal a mind broken by loneliness and longing, finding release in death by imagining the return home he had craved. There is profound pathos in the irony: the 'holiday' he has been waiting for is death, and in his final moments he is happy.
keyPoints: Mother sent Phatik away because he was troublesome — reveals she found him burdensome
At school: dull, beaten, mocked; aunt treated him with cold indifference
Anguish: homesickness, aunt's unkindness, school failures, lost books, illness
Ran away in rain, found collapsed with fever, brought back dying
'Holidays have come': delirious belief he is going home; death as the longed-for return; profound pathos

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

"The gardener
crooning,
It is your nature
to be small and cosy,
dome-topped, narrow.
Flaws of silver hair,
wrinkle, down hill now,
your nature
is to be small and cozy."

(i) Who does the 'gardener' represent in the poem? What is his relationship to the bonsai tree?
(ii) What does the bonsai's 'nature' to be 'small and cosy' symbolise? What is Marge Piercy's view of this 'nature'?
(iii) What does the mountain symbolise in the poem? What words does the poet use to emphasise the restriction imposed on the tree?
(iv) Explain the irony in the line 'How lucky, little tree, to have a pot to grow in'.
modelAnswer:
(i) The gardener represents patriarchal society — the system of male dominance that shapes and confines women's lives from birth. His relationship to the bonsai is one of control: he carefully prunes, whittles and stunts the tree's growth, crooning soothingly as he does so, making the restriction seem like care or even a gift.
(ii) The bonsai's 'nature' to be small and cosy symbolises the imposed domesticity forced upon women — the idea that women are naturally suited to a narrow, confined, domestic role. Piercy's view is that this 'nature' is entirely artificial, created by centuries of social conditioning and control, not by any genuine female nature.
(iii) The mountain symbolises the full natural potential of the tree and of women — freedom, grandeur and unchecked growth. The poem says the tree could have grown eighty feet tall, split by lightning. Words like 'prune', 'whittle' and 'dwarf' emphasise the deliberate, ongoing restriction imposed on its natural development.
(iv) The irony is bitter. 'How lucky, little tree, to have a pot to grow in' presents confinement as fortune, limitation as privilege. The gardener's crooning voice makes imprisonment sound like a gift. The irony lies in the contrast between the soothing, congratulatory tone and the reality: the pot is a prison that has robbed the tree of eighty feet of growth and its natural life.
keyPoints: Gardener = patriarchal society; relationship: control through pruning and conditioning
Bonsai's 'nature' = imposed domesticity; Piercy says it is artificial, not natural
Mountain = full natural potential, freedom; prune/whittle/dwarf emphasise restriction
Eighty feet tall, split by lightning — natural life denied
Irony: 'How lucky' — confinement presented as fortune; prison made to sound like a gift

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

"He will watch you without winking and he sees what you are thinking
And it's certain that he doesn't approve
Of hilarity and riot, so the folk are very quiet
When Skimble's about and on the move."

(i) Who are 'the folk' mentioned here? Why are they quiet?
(ii) What comforts does Skimble provide for the passengers in the sleeping car? Name at least three.
(iii) How does Skimble ensure the safety of the passengers during the journey? Give two examples.
(iv) What happens at Gallowgate? What does this reveal about Skimble's character?
modelAnswer:
(i) 'The folk' are the passengers travelling in the sleeping car of the Night Mail. They are quiet because Skimble watches everyone keenly — he 'sees what you are thinking' — and disapproves strongly of any noise, disorder or rowdiness. His watchful presence imposes a natural discipline.
(ii) Comforts Skimble provides: a cosy berth with the passenger's name written on the door; a neat, newly folded sheet; not a speck of dust in sight; a little basin for washing; lights that can be made bright or dim as preferred; a crank to open or shut the window; and a button to call for a breeze. (Any three are sufficient.)
(iii) For safety: Skimble patrols the train all night long without sleeping; he watches without winking, keeping an eye on everyone; he keeps away any mice that might disturb passengers; and at Dumfries he is ready to call in the police if anything is amiss.
(iv) At Gallowgate the passengers get out without having to wait, because Skimble has everything organised and ready for a smooth, quick departure. This reveals his thoroughness, efficiency and genuine helpfulness — he does not merely police the passengers but actively serves them, ensuring their journey ends as smoothly as it began.
keyPoints: 'Folk' = passengers in sleeping car; quiet because Skimble watches and disapproves of noise
Comforts: named berth, neat sheet, no dust, little basin, adjustable lights, window crank, breeze button (any 3)
Safety: patrols without sleeping, watches without winking, keeps away mice, summons police at Dumfries
Gallowgate: passengers depart without waiting — Skimble's efficiency and helpfulness
Reveals thoroughness and genuine care for passengers

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

BRUTUS: What means this shouting? I do fear, the people
Choose Caesar for their king.
CASSIUS: Ay, do you fear it?
Then must I think you would not have it so.
BRUTUS: I would not, Cassius; yet I love him well.
But wherefore do you hold me here so long?
What is it that you would impart to me?

(i) Where does this scene take place and on what occasion? How do Brutus and Cassius come to be alone together?
(ii) What does Brutus mean when he says he is 'with himself at war'? What is the conflict within him?
(iii) What two examples of Caesar's physical weakness does Cassius give to prove Caesar unworthy of power?
(iv) What physical disability does Caesar have? How does Cassius use the fact of Caesar's power to appeal to Brutus's pride?
modelAnswer:
(i) The scene takes place in a public place in Rome during the feast of Lupercal. The shouts they hear are the crowd cheering Caesar after Antony offers him the crown. Brutus and Cassius come to be alone because Cassius pulls Brutus back as the others leave — he has been watching Brutus's expression and seizes the opportunity to speak with him privately.
(ii) 'With himself at war' means Brutus is torn between two powerful loyalties: his deep personal love for Caesar on one side, and his love for Rome and his fear of tyranny on the other. He is in inner conflict — he cannot reconcile his affection for Caesar with his republican principles.
(iii) Cassius gives two examples: first, the Tiber swim, in which Caesar cried 'Help me, Cassius, or I sink!' and had to be rescued, showing physical weakness; second, the fever Caesar suffered in Spain, during which he shook and begged 'Give me some drink, Titinius', showing him to be frail and dependent — not the godlike figure Romans worship.
(iv) Caesar is deaf in his left ear (hence 'Come on my right hand, for this ear is deaf'). Cassius appeals to Brutus's pride by pointing out that Caesar is a man no stronger or better than Brutus himself, yet Caesar is to be called a god while Brutus walks under his great legs as a petty underling. This parallel between himself and Caesar stings Brutus's sense of his own dignity and worth.
keyPoints: Public place, feast of Lupercal; Cassius pulls Brutus back while others follow Caesar
'With himself at war': torn between love for Caesar and love for Rome/fear of tyranny
Physical weakness: Tiber swim ('Help me, Cassius, or I sink!'); fever in Spain ('Give me some drink')
Caesar deaf in left ear
Cassius appeals to Brutus's pride: Caesar no better than Brutus, yet Brutus walks as a petty underling

text:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

"The morning was still, the sky was serene, the air was fresh and clean. I noticed shimmering leaves and the soft shadows they made."

(i) Who is the writer of this journal entry? What is the significance of the date on which this entry is made?
(ii) How does the writer describe the morning before the explosion? What is the effect of this description?
(iii) What is the tone of the writing? How does the ending of the extract convey the horror of what has happened?
(iv) What do the 'shimmering leaves' and 'soft shadows' suggest about the writer's mood just before the catastrophe?
modelAnswer:
(i) The journal entry is written by Dr Michihiko Hachiya, a Japanese doctor who was in Hiroshima. The date is 6 August 1945 — the day the United States dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima, one of the most devastating events of the Second World War.
(ii) The writer describes the morning as still, serene and fresh, with shimmering leaves and soft shadows — a scene of tranquil, ordinary beauty. The effect of this description is to create a stark, terrible contrast with the destruction that follows: the more peaceful and beautiful the morning seems, the more shocking and unimaginable the catastrophe becomes.
(iii) The tone is calm and detached — almost clinical — as if the writer is observing the world with a doctor's precise, dispassionate eye. The ending conveys horror through its very silence and abruptness: words fail, and the stillness of the prose mirrors the stunned, eerie desolation that follows the blast, suggesting a shock too great for language.
(iv) The 'shimmering leaves' and 'soft shadows' suggest that the writer is in a peaceful, perhaps even contented mood — alert to small natural beauties, calm and unhurried. The irony is devastating: this ordinary morning pleasure is the last moment of the old world, seconds before annihilation. The beauty of the detail makes the subsequent horror all the more unbearable.
keyPoints: Dr Michihiko Hachiya; date = 6 August 1945, atomic bombing of Hiroshima
Morning described as still, serene, fresh — sharp contrast with destruction that follows
Tone: calm, detached, clinical; ending: silence and abruptness convey stunned desolation
Horror through absence of language — shock too great to describe
'Shimmering leaves/soft shadows': peaceful mood, alert to beauty — last moment before annihilation; irony
